analysis.one_liner: Lets the Labor Department fine employer health plans that shortchange mental health coverage.
analysis.headline: The Parity Enforcement Act never left the House Education and Labor Committee, dying without a markup or vote despite 19 cosponsors including one Republican.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires employer health plans to cover mental health and addiction treatment on par with physical health care, but the Department of Labor has no power to fine plans that break that rule. This bill would amend the Employee Retirement Income Security Act to give the Labor Department civil penalty authority over parity violations, taking effect for plan years starting at least a year after enactment. It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and was never scheduled for a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly half of Americans with private employer health coverage would gain a way to actually enforce their right to equal mental health and substance use benefits. Today, if a plan quietly charges higher copays or imposes stricter limits on mental health care than on other care, federal enforcement is essentially toothless; under this bill, the Labor Department could assess civil monetary penalties, giving plans a real financial reason to comply and giving people with depression, addiction, or other conditions coverage that works in practice.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends ERISA Section 502(c)(10) so the Department of Labor can enforce the mental health and substance use disorder parity requirements of section 712, alongside its existing authority over genetic information violations.
Enforcement would apply to group health plans for plan years beginning more than one year after enactment.
The bill also extends related penalty and notice provisions to cover the new parity authority, including through technical amendments to ERISA Section 502.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor group health plans and the insurers that administer them would bear the cost: plans that currently skimp on mental health and addiction benefits would face civil penalties, and bringing benefits into genuine parity could raise plan costs for employers, some of which might be passed to workers through premiums or wages.

drawbacks.text: Giving the Labor Department penalty authority over employer plans could raise the cost of offering health benefits, and some employers might respond by trimming coverage rather than expanding mental health benefits to full parity.

The bill covers only ERISA-governed group health plans, so it would not address parity in other coverage, and the penalty mechanism alone does not guarantee workers know their rights or can spot violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: parity on paper already exists; this bill supplies the missing enforcement teeth. The main cost falls on employers and insurers, and some of it could reach workers through benefit costs. The bill is narrow and targeted, but the one-sided outcome is that a modest, bipartisan enforcement fix never even received a committee hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross introduced the Parity Enforcement Act of 2019 on May 20, 2019, joined by Reps. Joe Courtney and Ann Kuster of New Hampshire.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction.
The full action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed.
The bill attracted 19 cosponsors: 18 of 231 House Democrats and 1 of 197 House Republicans.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and all bills not enacted by then expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and insurers that sponsor or administer group health plans are better off, because they continue to face no federal civil penalties when they cover mental health and addiction treatment less generously than other care. People with mental health conditions in employer plans are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers dodge parity fines

for.name: Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to give the Labor Department penalty authority over mental health parity violations.

for.name: Joe Courtney
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at introduction.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call splits exist; sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (18 of 231 Democrats versus 1 of 197 Republicans).

industries.note: Under current law these employers face no civil monetary penalties when they cover mental health or addiction treatment less generously than other care. This bill would expose them to Labor Department fines and the cost of bringing benefits into real parity, which is why their interest ran against the workers the bill would protect.

Insurers administer employer plans and share the cost pressure of parity enforcement, including fines and stricter benefit rules. They would have had to rework how mental health and substance use benefits are managed and limited.
